findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an acceptance criterion requiring ADR 0105 to record and resolve the load-bearing capability assertions: core-git `fast-import` (no `git filter-repo`) as the rewrite primitive, `push --force-with-lease` ref-CAS on git remotes, and the S3 `git-remote-s3` auto-doctor's never-discard-a-head resurrection hazard requiring an exclusive bundle-set replacement that bypasses it.
evidence: The portability AC only requires 'the N-day horizon as a portable config key (default 30d) with NO single-CI-provider trigger' — it does not require the ADR to name/verify the rewrite primitive or the per-backend publish-swap adapters whose portability is the actual bright-line risk.

The epic comment 'Design addendum 2' establishes the S3 resurrection hazard: 'A rewritten baseline pushed normally would be treated as just another divergent head and MERGED BACK — resurrecting the exact history we reclaimed' — a capability fact so load-bearing that its omission from the ADR would leave the C1-C5 no-resurrection proof unsound on the S3 backend, yet no AC requires the ADR to carry it.

docs/adr/0093 confirms the auto-doctor 'never discarding a head' invariant (src/rebar/_store/s3_doctor.py) that is precisely the resurrection vector — an unverified 'the backend behaves as assumed' assertion that T1(c) requires be resolved in the ADR that proves no-resurrection.
findings.finding: The load-bearing capability assertions on which the whole reclamation rests are stated in the parent epic's comments but are NOT required by any ADR acceptance criterion to be written down and resolved in ADR 0105 itself. The plan's own scope/ACs do not require the ADR to record that (a) core-git `git fast-import`/`git mktree`+`commit-tree` (not third-party `git filter-repo`) is the portable rewrite primitive, (b) `git push --force-with-lease=<ref>:<T0>` provides the ref-CAS publish-swap on git remotes, and (c) the S3 `git-remote-s3` backend has NO ref CAS and its non-interactive auto-doctor would MERGE BACK (resurrect) a normally-pushed rewrite — requiring an exclusive bundle-set replacement that bypasses the auto-doctor.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria (portability AC and C1-C5 AC)
scenarios: ADR 0105 is written proving C1-C5 no-resurrection while silently assuming a universal ref-CAS; an S3-backed store then resurrects reclaimed history because the auto-doctor merges the rewrite back.
An implementer trusts the ADR's portability claim, reaches for `git filter-repo` (not vendored), and finds the primitive unavailable.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an AC: 'The ADR names the history-rewrite primitive as core-git (git fast-import / mktree+commit-tree, no third-party git filter-repo) and, per backend, the publish-swap: git-ref --force-with-lease CAS for git remotes, and an exclusive push-locked bundle-set replacement bypassing the git-remote-s3 auto-doctor for the S3 backend — with the auto-doctor never-discard-a-head resurrection hazard cited (ADR 0093 / s3_doctor.py) and its bypass proven under C1-C5.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a scope item + acceptance criterion requiring ADR 0105 to consider prior art for its core pattern: relate the commit/tree-collapse + forced-remote-override model to the established 'never rewrite shared history / coordinate + hard-reset-to-remote' playbook and to how peer git-native trackers (git-bug, git-appraise, jujutsu) reclaim branch-log growth, justifying the novelty (or repackaging) explicitly.
evidence: Scope enumerates only internal mechanics: 'the horizon config key … the remote-reachability computation … the stale-clone detection + FORCED remote-override protocol … the C1-C5 causal-stability boundary … a proof that invariants I1-I9 still hold' — no prior-art/alternatives clause.

docs/concurrency.md already cites prior art for a related mechanism: 'The fix follows the universal peer pattern (git-bug, git-appraise, jujutsu): make recovery non-destructive' — establishing that this repo grounds store-history decisions in peer trackers, a norm this ADR's ACs do not carry forward.

Web (retrieved): 'The Golden Rule: Never Rewrite Shared History' (kindatechnical.com) and 'Rewriting Shared History Without Losing Friends' (deska.dev) document the established mitigations — force-with-lease + collaborators fresh-clone/hard-reset to remote — which the plan's 'forced remote-override' re-invents without naming the prior art it repackages.

The forced-override that discards >N-day-drifted local work is the plan's most novel/consequential choice; the golden-rule sources treat 'collaborators hard-reset to remote' as the accepted cost of any shared-history rewrite — the ADR should site its choice in that context rather than presenting it as sui generis.
findings.finding: The ADR's scope and acceptance criteria never require it to consider PRIOR ART for its novel core pattern — below-horizon commit/tree-collapse history reclamation on a shared, continuously-auto-pushed event-sourced branch, plus a forced remote-override that discards a stale clone's local work. This is a bright-line novel architecture, yet no scope item or AC asks the ADR to relate it to the well-established 'never rewrite shared history + coordinate + collaborators hard-reset to remote' playbook, or to how peer git-native distributed trackers (git-bug, git-appraise, jujutsu) handle branch-log/history growth.
findings.location: Scope paragraph and Acceptance Criteria (all six items)
scenarios: A future maintainer reads ADR 0105 as the standalone causal-stability contract and cannot tell whether the forced-override-discards-local-work model was chosen over, or is merely a rename of, the standard shared-history-rewrite recovery playbook.
S1-S3 implementers inherit a doctrine that never weighed peer-tracker approaches to log/history reclamation, risking reinvention.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an AC: 'The ADR includes a Prior Art / Alternatives Considered subsection that (1) names the established shared-history-rewrite recovery playbook (force-with-lease + collaborators reset-to-remote) its forced-override reuses, (2) surveys how peer git-native trackers (git-bug, git-appraise, jujutsu — already cited in docs/concurrency.md) manage branch-log/history growth, and (3) justifies commit/tree collapse + forced override as chosen over those alternatives.'
